2. Sensor alerts from an Iceberg table

Say you look after a plant's temperature sensors. When a machine runs hot for three minutes in a row, someone on call gets paged, and if the alert is wrong in either direction, it's their night or the machine that pays for it. You want an alert at every reading that is the third or more in a row above 30 °C. The sensors write a reading per device per minute to an Iceberg table, and the rule is iot-consecutive-threshold in the query catalogue (Azure Stream Analytics' MATCH_RECOGNIZE example). In SQL that is two LAGs over a window. Window queries are where engines quietly disagree. Three things go wrong in practice, and we'll run into each:
  • ties: two readings of a device at the same instant make "previous reading" ambiguous, and each engine picks one;
  • NaN: a glitching sensor sends NaN, and in SQL NaN > 30 is TRUE (NaN sorts above every number), while in Python and pandas it is False, so a prototype and the production job disagree;
  • warehouses without row order: Snowflake and Spark tables have no order to break ties with.
As in chapter 1, the job reads the source, states and proves a contract, runs on every engine, keeps up with new data and writes a sink.

1. The source: an Iceberg table of readings

Iceberg wants a catalog, so a small SQLite one in a temporary folder plays the part of Glue, a REST catalog or Unity. device_id and ts are required. Two of the devices are troublemakers: device 2 skipped a reading (NULL), and device 3 had a glitch and sent NaN. We'll see what each of them does to the alerts.

data.text/markdown:
2. The rule, and the first thing the checker says

Straight from the catalogue, three high readings in a row:

Think of whoever gets paged at 3 a.m. They'll assume that every alert means the temperature really is above 30, and that one hot minute pages them once, not three times. Those are reasonable things to rely on, so let's write them down and ask the checker. First, with no assumptions about the input:

⚠️ rows may tie in a window's ORDER BY, so the engine decides their order. Declare unique(...) on the partition and order columns of the input.
postcondition status
(_.temperature > 30) ❌ undetermined: rows may tie in a window's ORDER BY, and the engine orders them
unique(device_id, ts) ❌ undetermined: rows may tie in a window's ORDER BY
output column known values
device_id any integer
ts any timestamp
temperature a double > 30.0

Nothing is proved, not even temperature > 30, which is in the filter. The verdict is undetermined: if a device can send two readings with the same ts, which one is "previous" depends on how the engine breaks the tie, and engines break ties differently from run to run. The catalogue found this in 44 of its 139 queries (dedup, top-N, LAG over equal timestamps); it is the most common way for engines to disagree. The fix is to say what the source promises: at most one reading per device and minute. That's a promise the sensor team can make, and one we'll hold them to later.

3. The NaN glitch

With that key, we try again, and also ask that no alert is a NaN: the person paged needs a temperature, not a glitch.

postcondition status
(_.temperature > 30) ✅ proved
~_.temperature.isnan() ❌ TRUE or FALSE
unique(device_id, ts) ✅ proved
output column known values
device_id any integer
ts any timestamp
temperature a double > 30.0

temperature > 30 and the key are proved now. ~isnan() is refused, and the checker is right. In SQL, NaN > 30 is TRUE: NaN sorts above every number, so device 3's glitch counts as hot and pages someone. We'll want to rule that out. Python says the opposite, which is how a rule tested in pandas misbehaves in the warehouse:
So we say what a high reading is. NaN then breaks the run, like a missing reading does:

4. Both rules on the data

We put both versions side by side as nodes over the Iceberg source, and refresh them together with sv.group, so they see the same snapshot. The naive rule gets an empty contract, sv.transform(), which promises nothing but lets it read the source too. Building the alerts node proves its contract:

The naive rule alerts on device 3 because of the NaN; the contracted one doesn't. Device 2's missing reading breaks its run in both.

data.text/markdown:
5. Every engine, and the warehouses

The alerts may run on a laptop today and in the warehouse tomorrow. DuckDB, Polars and DataFusion run the checked plan with the same rows, whichever engine= the node is refreshed with. Snowflake and Spark tables have no row order, so sverify refuses to write a window for them unless you promise the order keys have no ties. The report's deterministic is exactly that promise, proved from the key, so it can be passed on:

data.text/html: "Snowflake tables have no row order, so FETCH and windows over a named table cannot follow the Lean model's list order (windows run with tie_free=True)"

data.text/markdown:
With tie_free=True the SQL is written. Without the key, deterministic would be False, and passing tie_free=True anyway would be an unproved promise.

6. New readings, and a sensor that sends twice

A window isn't incrementally maintainable (yet), and the node says so up front instead of maintaining it incorrectly. Such a node is recomputed and diffed on each refresh; its change still flows to the sink and to nodes downstream:

console.name: stdout
console.text: alerts: readings@v1; recomputed (not incrementally maintainable (left join, fetch or window))

data.text/markdown: We store the node in an Iceberg sink with .write, and its first refresh writes the first state. The sink keeps the contract in the table properties and in every snapshot summary:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
alerts:
  computed
  requires readings: unique(device_id, ts) (checked on data)
  wrote alerts from readings@v1: created v1, 1 row(s) written, 0 deleted

data.text/markdown: Device 2 keeps running hot, and two more readings arrive. Iceberg appends are read from the files they added, and the keys of the new rows are checked against the rows kept:

  readings@v1→v2: 2 insert(s), 0 delete(s); Δ trusted as the files Iceberg appends v1→v2 added
  requires readings: unique(device_id, ts) (checked on data)
  view alerts: readings@v2
  wrote alerts from readings@v2: append v2, 1 row(s) written, 0 deleted

data.text/markdown: Device 2's 12:03 reading doesn't alert (12:01 was missing); 12:04 does. Then device 1 sends two readings for 12:04. That is exactly the case the key rules out, and the one that would make the alerts depend on the engine. The refresh refuses the batch, and nothing changes: the node and the sink stay at the last good version, and the next refresh retries from there.

data.text/markdown:
What you got

You now have alerts the on-call engineer can rely on. The checker found two real bugs before anything ran, an alert that depended on how ties were broken and a NaN reading that would have paged someone, and nobody was woken up for either. The key is checked on every batch, so a sensor that sends twice stops the job instead of making it engine-dependent. The same plan runs on DuckDB, Polars and DataFusion, and you get Snowflake or Spark SQL only once the tie-freedom it needs is proved. The window node is honest about not being incremental, and stays up to date by recomputation, with its change written to the sink. Next up: An orders mart in SQL and Ibis, where a dashboard's dbt tests become a contract. Windows and ties are covered in depth in Windows and ASOF joins, NaN and other double semantics in Doubles, time and text.
